1a:
Award the point if the answer conveys, in substance, that the serialization performed on the copied result does not propagate back to the original reply object — i.e., because `deepcopy(result)` produces an independent copy, mutating the data field on that copy leaves the reply's corresponding data unchanged. Exact naming is not required: an explanation that refers to "the data field," "the reply," "the original dict," or a generic shared-reference/independent-copy account is fully acceptable, and is just as creditable as one that names `result[DATA]` and `reply.result[DATA]` explicitly. What matters is that the answer ties the deepcopy to the specific consequence that the serialization step does not show up in the original/reply object.

Deduct 1 point only if the answer never conveys this non-propagation of the serialization step — for example, if it describes deepcopy only in the abstract (what deepcopy does in general, or that it avoids side effects) without making clear that the serialization applied to the copy is not reflected back in the reply's data.
1b:
**Sub-item 1b (−2 points if triggered): "discusses implications on transaction types other than SCHEMA or ISSUER_KEY"**

Deduct the 2 points only when the answer asserts some positive effect or consequence of the deepcopy for a transaction type that is not SCHEMA or ISSUER_KEY — either by naming such a type and claiming something happens to it, or by generalizing the behavior beyond the two in-scope types without naming any, e.g. "this applies to every transaction," "any reply's result is affected," "all ledger writes." Such unnamed generalizations count as asserting implications for other transaction types and are deducted just as a named claim would be.

Do not deduct when other transaction types appear solely in a negative or scoping clause that confines the effect to SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY — for example, "for other transaction types this makes no difference" or "only SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY results are serialized this way." Contrastive statements of that kind reinforce the correct scope rather than discussing implications elsewhere, so they are no_deduct. Likewise, an answer that simply confines itself to SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY, saying nothing about other types, is no_deduct.
2a:
Award the point (no deduct) whenever the answer, in any form, raises the ledger as a consumer of the serialized DATA — i.e., it names a concrete destination for the modified/serialized copy (the ledger, the stored/written transaction, what gets written out) rather than merely asserting that the mutation would be visible "somewhere," in "side effects," or in "other parts of the system." This item asks only whether the topic is discussed, so imprecise, hedged, or even partially wrong phrasing still counts as "mentioned"; the claim need not be stated accurately or confidently. It also still counts when the answer mentions the graph alongside the ledger, provided it is the modified/serialized copy that it says goes to the ledger.

Deduct the point when the answer never identifies the ledger (or the stored/written-out txn) as where the serialized data ends up — for example, when it only traces the preserved original back to the graph and never ties the serialized copy to the ledger, or when it speaks only generically about the serialization having effects elsewhere in the system without naming a concrete consumer.
2b:
**Sub-item 2b — "the data serialization will not be reflected in the graph" (1 point).**

Award no_deduct only if the answer specifically identifies the graph store as the destination that does *not* receive the serialized data — i.e., it names "the graph," "graph storage," "the OrientDB graph," `storeTxnInGraph`, or equivalent explicit graph terminology, and states that this path gets the pre-serialization copy (`result`) rather than the serialized `reply.result`. The naming of the graph is what satisfies this item; a generic description of the same mechanism does not.

Deduct the point if the answer never names the graph store, even when it correctly describes the split behavior in other terms — for example, if it only says the unserialized copy goes to "other consumers," "the client" or "the reply," "the in-memory copy," or "downstream code," or otherwise gestures at a non-ledger consumer without identifying it as the graph. Also deduct if the graph is not mentioned at all in connection with the missing serialization.
